newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia to seek to overcome U.S. trade gap.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia to seek to overcome U.S. trade gap.

text.p: Australia will try to reduce access barriers to U.S. markets in an effort to even up the country's largest trade imbalance, deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said on Tuesday.

Fischer, who is also Trade Minister, said he would hold further talks with U.S. Trade Representative-designate Charlene Barshefsky this year, although he said some progress on access barriers had been made.
"We remain concerned about the Export Enhancement Programme for grain subsidisation and the DEEP (Dairy Export Enhancement) programme," he said in an interview on Reuters Financial Television.
"There are still areas of great difficulty which we will continue to negotiate on."
Fischer said Asia remained Australia's top priority in terms of foreign affairs and trade following last year's change of government to a Liberal-National Party coalition.
"(But) it's not a case of Asia full stop, it's a case of Asia and the rest of the world," he said.
Australia enjoyed a trade surplus with Asia as a regional grouping, but had its "worst" trade imbalance with the United States.
Australia recorded a balance of merchandise trade deficit with the United States in 1995/96 ended June of A$12.97 billion.
"There are cyclical and other structural reasons associated with that, but I am not happy about it and we would want to further expand our export effort to the U.S.," Fischer said.
Asked about the outlook for the imbalance to improve, he said: "If there was absolutely no access barriers, it would close up quite rapidly."
Fischer noted that the Australian and U.S. governments enjoyed a particuarly good bilateral relationship.
"I do not see insurmountable problems, but it is the speed at which some of these problems are addressed which is always very pertinent, very relevant."

Responding to domestic criticism that Australia had acted too quickly to cut trade barriers, Fischer said the government closely consulted industry and recognised there was no such thing as a level international playing field.
"We will therefore be pragmatic, hard edged, as we adminster the detail of our trade policy," he said. "We will do it on a sensible basis heading in that general direction of trade liberalisation."
Asked about controversial independent politician Pauline Hanson, Fischer said he respected her right to speak out.
But he stressed that the Australian government and parliament supported the building of trade, investment and tourism links with Asia, as well as a non-discriminatory immigration policy.
"Her place in the sun will wax and wane, but the Australian government's official policy and the policy of the Australian parliament remains absolute," he said.
Hanson has created controversy by calling for cuts to Asian immigration to Australia, to foreign aid and to welfare for Aborigines.
